Web pages draw their own. Can I pick the material from Terminal? Not yet. diatweaks turns it on and off, and Settings picks the material.

title: Keep Windows Active
text: Keeps a Dia window's deep shadow, sidebar color and window buttons after you click into another app, so screenshots and recordings look the same whatever has focus. It's experimental. Tabs in the sidebar Tabs at the top :---::---: Why use it macOS dims a window's shadow, sidebar and buttons when another app has focus. That dulls screenshots and screen recordings when you click into a recorder or notes app. Use it when you capture Dia and want it to look the same whatever has focus. Skip it if you rely on the dimming to see which window gets your typing. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Keep Windows Active. Or run: sh diatweaks enable keepWindowsActive Good to know This tweak is experimental. Every Dia window looks focused while it's on, so the look no longer tells you which one gets your typing, and focus rings can show in windows you aren't typing in. Settings and other small panels aren't affected.

title: Drag Window from Page
text: Drag an empty spot near the top of a page to move the window, like a title bar. With the toolbar and sidebar hidden, a page's own header is often all there is to grab. Why use it With the toolbar and sidebar hidden, Dia has no title bar to grab, so moving the window is awkward. Use it with the toolbar or sidebar hidden, or any time you want a bigger target to drag from. Nothing changes for links, buttons or text near the top. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Drag Window from Page. Or run: sh diatweaks enable dragWindowFromPage FAQ Which parts of a page can I drag? Anywhere in the top 56 points of the page where the pointer is a plain arrow. Links and buttons show a hand and text shows an I-beam, so those stay clickable and selectable as usual. Can I still click those empty spots? Yes. If you let go without moving, the page gets the click as normal. Does it work with tabs at the top? Yes, in both layouts, with or without the toolbar.

title: Window Corners
text: Rounds browser windows to 26 points, like apps with a toolbar on macOS 26, or to any radius you pick down to square, instead of the smaller corners Dia's windows get. The page's corners that meet the window's grow with them so the gap around the page stays even, while the ones by the sidebar keep Dia's size. The sidebar that floats over the page when it's hidden, the pinned tabs and buttons in the window's corners, and the toolbar buttons in the page's top corners, like Chat, round to match. Toolbar buttons only round the corner they share. Tabs in the sidebar Tabs at the top :---::---: Why use it Dia's windows have smaller corners than most macOS 26 apps, so Dia looks out of place next to them. This rounds them to match, and keeps the page's corners in step. Handy if you want Dia to look native on macOS 26. If you prefer a sharper look, set the radius lower, down to square. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Window Corners. Or run: sh diatweaks enable windowCorners Options On the same page, once it's on: - Radius: a slider from 0 to 26 points, 26 to begin with. 26 matches macOS 26 and 10 matches macOS 11 to 15. The page's corners follow, and with Edge-to-Edge Web Pages a square window has a square page. 0 is a 1 point radius, the smallest macOS draws. FAQ Does it work with tabs at the top? Yes. With Hide Window Controls on, the pinned tabs sit in the corner and round to match it. Does it work with Edge-to-Edge Web Pages? Yes. The page reaches the window's edge with the same corners as the window.

title: Dock Click Shows Existing Window
text: Click Dia's Dock icon from another Desktop and macOS takes you to the Dia window you already have, like other apps, instead of opening a new one. Why use it Dia opens a new window when the Desktop you're on has none of its windows, so a Dock click from Desktop 2 piles a second window on top of the one waiting on Desktop 1. With this on, the click goes to that window. Use it if you keep Dia on one Desktop and click its icon from the others. Skip it if you want a fresh window on every Desktop. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Dock Click Shows Existing Window. Or run: sh diatweaks enable dockClickWindow The macOS setting it needs In System Settings → Desktop & Dock, turn on When switching to an application, switch to a Space with open windows for the application. It's on unless you've turned it off. With it off, macOS wouldn't show the window, so this tweak steps aside and Dia opens a new window as usual. Good to know - It only acts when Dia has a window on another Desktop and none on this one. A Dock click while a window is here, or on a minimized or hidden Dia, works as before. - If Dia has no windows at all, the click opens a new one as usual. - Little Dia's small windows don't count. Only Dia's regular windows do. - With several Dia windows on other Desktops, you go to the one you used last. FAQ Does it change anything with the tweak off? No. Dia opens a new window, as it always has.

title: Hide Window Controls
text: Hides the close, minimize and zoom buttons. ⌘W, ⌘M and the Window menu still work, and you can still drag the window by the sidebar or tab bar. Tabs in the sidebar Tabs at the top :---::---: Why use it The close, minimize and zoom buttons take up space at the top of the sidebar or tab bar, and most people close windows with ⌘W anyway. Use it for a cleaner, tighter top edge. You can't close a window by clicking, so skip it if you do that often. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Hide Window Controls. Or run: sh diatweaks enable hideTrafficLights FAQ Why does the sidebar show my profile's name? That's what Dia shows in the space the buttons leave. Clicking it switches profiles as before. Does it work with tabs at the top? Yes. The pinned tabs move into the space.

title: App Icon
text: Changes the icon Dia shows in the Dock. Pick Dia's own icon, Classic (the old gradient icon), or one of eight colors. It follows the icon style you choose in System Settings. Why use it Dia has one icon. A different one can suit your Dock or your wallpaper, and the change shows right away, with no relaunch. - Handy if you want Dia to stand out less, or more. - Skip it if you like Dia's own icon. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on App Icon. Or run: sh diatweaks enable appIcon Options The menu under the switch in Settings lists the icons. - Dia: Default, which is Dia's own icon, and Classic. - Colors: Blue, Green, Neutral, Orange, Pink, Purple, Red or Yellow. How each looks Every icon in each icon style, in the Dock. Light Dark Clear Light Clear Dark Default Classic Blue Green Neutral Orange Pink Purple Red Yellow FAQ Does it work with the Dark, Clear and Tinted icon styles? Yes. Every icon works in Default, Dark, Clear and Tinted. Change the style in System Settings, and the icon follows. Do I need to relaunch Dia? No. The Dock icon changes in about a tenth of a second. If Dia was set up before this tweak existed, turning it on the first time may ask you to relaunch once. Why is my icon a little off in Clear? If you pick a color while the Clear style is on, the color can look a bit different until the style changes next. What happens when I turn it off? Dia's own icon comes back.

title: Allow 1Password
text: The 1Password extension connects to the 1Password app in Dia again. Without it, a patched Dia gets stuck on "waiting for potential partner browser authorization". Why use it If you use 1Password, its browser extension stops working in a patched Dia, so you can't fill or save logins from it. Turn it on if 1Password is your password manager. The tradeoff is the original Dia flashing in the Dock for about half a second each time the extension connects. Turn it on It's off by default. Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Allow 1Password. Or run: sh diatweaks enable onePassword Then unlock the 1Password app. The extension picks it up within a minute. FAQ Why does a second Dia flash in the Dock? 1Password's helper only talks to browsers whose signature it knows, and a patched Dia is signed on your Mac. It checks once, as it starts. So each time the extension connects, usually once as Dia opens, DiaTweaks opens the original Dia it keeps, without windows, just long enough to start the helper, then quits it. Its icon shows in the Dock for about half a second. After that the extension talks to 1Password's helper directly, and nothing stays running. It's the same hand-off Allow iCloud Passwords uses, with two differences. 1Password's helper only reads apps under /Applications, so DiaTweaks keeps an instant copy of the original Dia in a hidden /Applications/.DiaTweaks folder, and refreshes it when Dia updates. And the helper checks its browser a moment after it starts, so the original Dia stays open for a third of a second longer. Uninstalling DiaTweaks deletes the folder. Does it work with tabs at the top? Yes. It doesn't change anything you see in Dia. Why did it switch itself off? It checks its setup when you turn it on and each time Dia opens: 1Password's browser support and the files DiaTweaks keeps. If something's missing, it sets it up again, up to three times. If that doesn't fix it, it switches itself off and an alert says what's wrong, like 1Password not having set up its browser support yet, or DiaTweaks needing to be installed again.

title: Allow iCloud Passkeys
text: Lets sites sign you in with passkeys saved in Apple Passwords (iCloud Keychain). It's experimental, and off by default since it opens the original Dia for a moment each time. Why use it If your passkeys are in Apple Passwords, a patched Dia can't offer them, so sites that need a passkey leave you stuck. Turn it on if you sign in to sites with iCloud passkeys. The tradeoff is a brief second Dia window behind the Touch ID prompt each time, and it is experimental. Why this is needed Apple only lets a browser use your iCloud passkeys if that browser has Apple's permission. Dia has it. But that permission is tied to Dia exactly as The Browser Company shipped it, and the moment DiaTweaks changes Dia, macOS no longer counts it as the browser Apple approved. Without this tweak, sites that ask for a passkey in a patched Dia can't see the ones in Apple Passwords. Only Apple can give that permission, and it can't be added back afterwards. So there's no way to make the patched Dia reach your passkeys by itself. How it works DiaTweaks already keeps a copy of the original, unchanged Dia on your Mac, because it builds the patched Dia from it. That original still has Apple's permission. So when a site asks for a passkey: 1. The original Dia opens in a small window, just the size of the Touch ID prompt, and goes to the same site. 2. The Touch ID prompt appears on top of it, so the prompt is mostly all you see. 3. You approve with Touch ID, like in any browser. 4. The site in your Dia gets the passkey, and the small window closes by itself. We've tried to make it feel as normal as we can. The window is tiny and sits behind the prompt, it's muted, it skips Dia's intro, and it signs in with your Dia account on its own. It's still a second Dia opening for a few seconds, and you might notice it in the Dock. There isn't a smoother way to do this without Apple's permission. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches, switch on Allow iCloud Passkeys, and relaunch Dia when it asks. Or run: sh diatweaks enable passkeys FAQ It says "Couldn't write … NativeMessagingHosts: You don't have permission" Dia only reads extension helpers from ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome, and on your Mac that folder isn't yours to write to, usually because an installer or a command run with sudo made it. Take it back by running this in Terminal and typing your Mac password when asked: sh sudo chown -R "$(whoami)" "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome" && chmod -R u+w "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome" Then turn the switch on again. Chrome keeps working as before, since the folder still belongs to you. Is it safe? Yes. Your passkeys never leave Apple Passwords, and each one still needs your Touch ID or password, the same as in Safari or Chrome. The original Dia is the one The Browser Company signed, untouched. It only opens the site that asked, and it quits as soon as you're done. Why is it slow the first time? The original Dia has to start up, which takes a few seconds. After that the prompt shows up quickly. Why doesn't a site suggest my passkey in its sign-in field? Some sites offer your passkey as soon as you click their sign-in field. That's off here, or the original Dia would open every time you visited one of those pages. Use the site's "Sign in with a passkey" button instead. It asked me to sign in to Dia. The original Dia normally signs in with your Dia account by itself. If it ever can't, sign in with your Dia email in the window that opens, and your passkey carries on after. It won't ask again. Why is there an extension called DiaTweaks Passkeys? That's how the patched Dia hands passkey requests to the original one. It's there while this tweak is on and goes away when you turn it off and relaunch. Do passkeys from 1Password or Bitwarden work? They come from their own browser extensions, not Apple Passwords, so this tweak doesn't change how they work. Why did it switch itself off? It checks its setup when you turn it on and each time Dia opens: its extension's files, the file that tells the extension where to connect, and the files DiaTweaks keeps. If something's missing, it sets it up again, up to three times. If that doesn't fix it, it switches itself off and an alert says what's wrong, like a file not being writable, another app having replaced it, or DiaTweaks needing to be installed again.

title: Allow iCloud Passwords
text: Apple's iCloud Passwords extension fills and saves your Apple Passwords in Dia again. Without it, a patched Dia gets "iCloud Passwords couldn't connect to a helper application". Why use it If you keep passwords in Apple Passwords, Apple's iCloud Passwords extension fails in a patched Dia, so you can't fill or save them. Turn it on if you use that extension. The tradeoff is the original Dia flashing in the Dock for about half a second as the extension connects. Turn it on It's off by default. Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Allow iCloud Passwords. Or run: sh diatweaks enable icloudPasswords Then add iCloud Passwords from the Chrome Web Store and click its icon. If it asks for a code, type the 6-digit code macOS shows you. It works for Better Passwords too, which talks to the same Apple helper. Set it up as its site says, then turn this on. While it's on, Better Passwords' own setup file for Chrome's folder is kept aside and put back when you turn it off. It works for Open Passwords too. Install its extension; you don't need its helper app, since DiaTweaks starts Apple's helper for it. If you have the helper app, its setup file is kept aside the same way while this is on. FAQ It says "Couldn't write … NativeMessagingHosts: You don't have permission" Dia only reads extension helpers from ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome, and on your Mac that folder isn't yours to write to, usually because an installer or a command run with sudo made it. Take it back by running this in Terminal and typing your Mac password when asked: sh sudo chown -R "$(whoami)" "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome" && chmod -R u+w "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome" Then turn the switch on again. Chrome keeps working as before, since the folder still belongs to you. Why doesn't Better Passwords' setup reach Dia? Dia reads these setup files only from Chrome's folder, ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts, not from Dia's own. With this on, DiaTweaks writes the file Better Passwords needs there, whether or not Chrome is installed. Why does a second Dia flash in the Dock? macOS only lets Apple's password helper start under the Dia Apple approved, and it only checks as the helper starts. So each time the extension connects, usually once per profile as Dia opens, DiaTweaks opens the original Dia it keeps, without windows, just long enough to start the helper, then quits it. Its icon shows in the Dock for about half a second. After that the extension talks to Apple's helper directly. Why does the pairing window say "(null)"? Apple's helper names the browser after the app that started it, and by then the original Dia has quit. Pairing still works. Does it work with tabs at the top? Yes. It doesn't change anything you see in Dia. Why did it switch itself off? It checks its setup when you turn it on and each time Dia opens: Apple's helper, the file that tells the extension where to connect, and the files DiaTweaks keeps. If something's missing, it sets it up again, up to three times. If that doesn't fix it, it switches itself off and an alert says what's wrong, like that file not being writable, another app having replaced it, or DiaTweaks needing to be installed again.

title: Peek on Shift-Click
text: Shift-click a link to preview it in a card over the page, like Arc. The card grows out of the link you clicked, and shrinks back into it when you close it. Use it Hold Shift and click a link. Holding Shift over a link starts loading it, so the page is usually ready by the time you click. - Close it: click outside the card, press Escape or ⌘W, or click × beside it. It shrinks back into the link. - Open it as a tab: press ⌘O or click the expand button. The card grows to fill the window and becomes a tab. - Open it beside the page: click the split button to put it in a split view. The tab you peeked from shows a small badge while the card is open. Why use it Opening a link in a new tab pulls you away from the page you were reading, and you have to find your way back. Use it to check an article, a profile or a search result and then dismiss it, or to keep it as a tab with ⌘O if it's worth it. Turn it on It's off by default. Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Peek on Shift-Click. Or run: sh diatweaks enable peek Options On the same page, under Options: Option What it does To begin with --------- Darken the page behind How dark the page behind the card gets 45% Speed How fast the card opens and closes, from 25% to 300% 90% Genie effect The card bends as it travels, like a window going into the Dock. Switch it off for a plain zoom On Also under Options: - Peek from Pinned Tabs opens links that leave a pinned tab's site in Peek instead of a new tab. - Drag Links to Peek shows a small card above a link you drag; drop the link on it to open it in Peek. FAQ Why doesn't Shift-click do anything right after Dia starts? Peek starts once you open or switch to a tab. Do that once and it works from then on. Can I have more than one card open? No, one per window. Close the card or open it as a tab before you peek at another link.

title: Peek from Pinned Tabs
text: With Peek on Shift-Click on, a link that leaves a pinned tab's site opens in Peek, like Arc, instead of in a new tab. Links on the same site still open in the pinned tab. Why use it A pinned tab is meant to stay on one site. Without this, a link that leaves the site opens a new tab and adds clutter next to your pins. Use it for pinned mail, chat or feed tabs where you often follow links out. Turn it off if you want those links as normal tabs. Turn it on It's on by default once Peek on Shift-Click is on. To change it, open Dia → Settings → Patches → Peek on Shift-Click and, under Options, use the Peek from Pinned Tabs switch. Or run: sh diatweaks enable peekPinnedLinks Needs Peek on Shift-Click. Settings greys out this switch until that's on, and diatweaks enable peekPinnedLinks offers to turn it on too. FAQ How do I keep the page? Press ⌘O or click the expand button beside the card, as with any Peek.

title: Drag Links to Peek
text: With Peek on Shift-Click on, start dragging a link and a small card appears just above it. Drop the link on the card to open it in Peek, no Shift needed, so you can peek with one hand. The card looks and moves like the ones Dia shows when you drag a tab into the page to split it: it grows and turns blue as the link comes near, and leans toward the pointer. Why use it Shift-click needs a key held down while you click. Dragging is a one-handed way to peek, handy on a trackpad when your other hand is busy. Use it if you already drag links around, for example to the sidebar. It only reacts to links, so it stays out of the way otherwise. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches → Peek on Shift-Click and, under Options, switch on Drag Links to Peek. Or run: sh diatweaks enable peekDragLinks Needs Peek on Shift-Click. Settings greys out this switch until that's on, and diatweaks enable peekDragLinks offers to turn it on too. FAQ Can I still drag links to other places? Yes. Drop it anywhere but the card, like the sidebar to open it as a tab, and Dia handles it as usual. The card only takes links dropped on it. What about dragging text or images? The card shows only for links to web pages. Dragging selected text brings up nothing.

title: Little Dia
text: Opens links from other apps, like Slack, Discord or Mail, in a small window instead of a new tab, like Little Arc. You can also right-click any link in a page and choose Open Link in Little Dia, or open a blank one from File → New Little Dia Window. The window has close, back, forward, reload and an address you can edit, and Open in Dia keeps the page as a tab. Why use it Most links you click in a chat or an email are a quick look. Without this, each one lands as a tab in your main window and brings Dia to the front. With it, the page opens over the app you clicked it in, and closing it takes you straight back there. Skip it if you'd rather every link end up as a tab. Turn it on Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Little Dia, then relaunch Dia when it asks. Or run: sh diatweaks enable littleDia Use it Click a link in another app, or right-click a link in a page in Dia and choose Open Link in Little Dia. It sits with the other Open Link items. To start from an empty window, choose File → New Little Dia Window or press ⌥⌘N. It opens a blank page in your current profile with the address ready to type. Both show only while Little Dia is on. In the small window: - ✕, ⌘W or Escape closes it and goes back to the app you came from. - Open in Dia or ⌘O moves the page to a tab in your main window. - ⌄, next to Open in Dia, lists your profiles with their dots, as Dia's Move to Profile does. Pick one to move the page to a tab in that profile instead. It shows when you have more than one profile. - Click the address, or press ⌘L, to type another address or search with your search engine. - ⌘R reloads. Hold Option as you click a link to open it in a tab as usual. A link on the page that would open a new tab opens in the small window instead, so nothing piles up out of sight. ⌘-click still opens a tab behind, in your main window, and a sign-in window a page opens still opens on its own. Options - Close with Escape: on by default. - Window Width and Window Height: the size it opens at, centred on the screen with the pointer. A size larger than the screen opens as large as fits. FAQ Am I signed in to sites in the small window? Yes. It's Dia's own popup window, the one sites get from window.open, so it uses the profile of your front window and its logins. What's the "DiaTweaks Little Dia" extension in my extensions? Only Dia's browser engine can make the small window, so a small extension makes it when a link comes in. It reads nothing on your pages. If you turn it off, links open in tabs again. Which links does it leave alone? Links you click in Dia itself, links you Option-click, and anything that isn't a web address, like mailto: links. To send a link in Dia to the small window, right-click it and choose Open Link in Little Dia. Does Open in Dia keep my place on the page? It opens the same address in a new tab, so the page loads again. A form you were filling in won't carry over. What if Dia was hidden? Only the small window shows. Close it and Dia hides again. Open in Dia, or picking a profile, brings your windows back with the page. Is the small window still there after I quit Dia? No. Like Little Arc, it closes with Dia and doesn't come back.

title: Close with Escape
text: Press Escape to close the Little Dia window and go back to the app the link came from. Why use it A quick look at a link should take one key to dismiss, the way it does in Little Arc. Turn it off if you use sites where Escape matters, like a dialog or a game, since with this on the page never sees Escape. Turn it on It's on by default once Little Dia is on. To change it, open Dia → Settings → Patches → Little Dia and, under Options, use the Close with Escape switch. Or run: sh diatweaks enable littleDiaEscapeCloses Needs Little Dia. Settings greys out this switch until that's on, and diatweaks enable littleDiaEscapeCloses offers to turn it on too. FAQ What if I'm typing an address? Escape cancels the typing first. Press it again to close the window. In full screen, Escape is left to the page.

title: Hide Link Address
text: Hides the address that shows at the bottom of the page when you point at a link. Why use it Dia shows a link's address in a bar at the bottom of the page when you point at it, which can cover content and distract. Use it for a cleaner page. You lose the quick check of where a link goes, so skip it if you use that to spot suspicious links. Turn it on It's off by default. Open Dia → Settings → Patches and switch on Hide Link Address. Or run: sh diatweaks enable hideLinkAddress Works with Peek on Shift-Click. Holding Shift over a link still starts loading it with the address hidden.

title: Discoveries
text: What we've learned about how Dia is built while making tweaks, and what worked when changing it. Class names are as they appear in a view dump (com.diapatches.dev.dump), and may change with any Dia update. title: Reading Dia's State
text: Part of Discoveries. Swift fields Most of Dia is Swift. -safeSwiftValueForKey: (from AXCoreUtilities, loaded in every AppKit app) reads a Swift property by name, such as spaceID, itemViews or isSelected. Swift collections come back as __SwiftValue Dictionaries usually bridge, but arrays often don't. Calling count or other NSArray methods on one crashes Dia. Parse its description instead, for example with a UUID regex. Dictionaries keyed by a Swift struct Keys such as SpaceID describe themselves as the ID, so [key description] gives you a string to compare. Lazy properties They're stored as $__lazy_storage_$_name, for example the profile dot $__lazy_storage_$_dotView. Setting Swift properties class_getInstanceVariable finds a Swift class's stored properties by name. An object one, like the command bar's font, can be assigned through a __strong pointer at its address, which ARC retains and releases as usual.

title: Window and Page
text: Part of Discoveries. The window Corners Dia's windows have no toolbar, so macOS gives them 16 point corners rather than the 26 points of macOS 26 apps. The private -_setCornerRadius: followed by -_updateWindowCornerMask changes them. The background is tiled WindowFrameBackgroundView holds several WindowBackgroundBaseView tiles of NSVisualEffectView around the page, not one view behind it. Each tile blurs on its own, so the seams flash while the sidebar slides. Giving every tile the whole window's frame removes the seams, and the color doesn't change. The theme color is a separate layer WindowBackgroundOverlayTintView sits above the tiles. To see through the window: - hide it - set window.opaque = NO and backgroundColor = clearColor - set the tiles to NSVisualEffectBlendingModeBehindWindow and NSVisualEffectStateActive, or they go flat when Dia isn't in front Inside the tint The tint holds a white or black wash, an ARCUI.BackgroundColorView at 70%, under a gradient of the profile's color at about 36%. A profile with no color still gets the gradient, as 3% grey. The wash is what covers the material, so hide only it to see through the window and keep the profile's color. Two copies of the tint The selected tab draws its own small WindowBackgroundOverlayTintView. When looking for the window's tint, only take one whose grandparent is the theme frame. Glass NSGlassEffectView has 24 private variants, set through _variant. Once drawn, a glass view keeps the variant it had, so make a new view to change variant. Dia's own toasts Dia 1.56 shows its own toasts, such as "Copied Current URL" after ⇧⌘C, in a _TtC11DiaToastsV210ToastPanel. Older versions don't have the class, so checking for it tells whether a tweak's own toast would show twice. Prompts are popovers Dia's downloads list (DownloadsButton.DownloadsMenuViewController) and the "not working correctly?" prompt after a few reloads (NavigationBar.AdBlockReloadNudgeContentViewController) are NSPopovers. To stop one, hook -[NSPopover showRelativeToRect:ofView:preferredEdge:] and skip it when contentViewController is that class. The page The rounded page It's an ARCUI.FlippedView inside ContentContainerView. Its layer's cornerRadius does the clipping. Different corners need cornerRadii, not a mask Dia crossfades a page that has a mask whenever it resizes. CALayer's private cornerRadii takes four sizes, in on-screen order from the top left, and animates like any property. Setting cornerRadius afterwards doesn't reset them. If all four are 0, Core Animation stops using them and clips to cornerRadius again, so a page that should be square goes round. Use 0.01 for a square corner. Shadow and border are paths An ARCUI.ShadowView draws a shadowPath, masked by a CAShapeLayer so the shadow only shows outside the page, plus a CAShapeLayer stroke for the border. All three have Dia's corner shape baked in, and need reshaping with the page. Dia animates those paths itself It uses the keys pathAnimation and shadowPathAnimation. A separate animation of your own drifts out of step. Instead: - reshape the animation's fromValue and toValue as Dia adds it (-addAnimation:forKey:) - reshape paths as Dia sets them (-setPath:, -setShadowPath:) Changing them later in layout shows Dia's shape for one frame. Mask layers have no superlayer Walking up from a layer won't find the page it belongs to. Keep a weak map from each layer you change to its page. Animation starts from the screen Dia often starts an animation from a path you set earlier. Remember the paths you set, and map them back to Dia's own before reshaping again. Sidebar show and hide Dia sets the page's frame inside an NSAnimationContext lasting 0.25 seconds. Read duration and timingFunction in the frame setter to match it. The white strip The strip at the page's edge while it resizes is Chromium redrawing the page a few frames late. It happens in stock Dia. The link address bubble The address that shows when you point at a link is StatusText.StatusTextView, in a StatusTextContainerView along the bottom of the page's container. Taking turns with Dia on a frame A tweak that sets a view's frame during layout, after Dia has set it, can start a fight: Dia sets its own back, the tweak sets it again, and once the passes outnumber the views in the window, AppKit throws its layout loop exception and Dia quits. It happened entering and leaving full screen with Edge-to-Edge, and while the menu bar slides in with Compact Sidebar Header, 8 to 100 seconds after launch. DPMayAdjust lets a tweak change a view's frame 8 times in one run loop turn, then leaves Dia's frame and lays the window out again once the run loop has waited. Colors with alpha keep one appearance [NSColor.labelColor colorWithAlphaComponent:] is fixed to the appearance it was made in, so it stays white on a light background. For one that follows the view, use +colorWithName:dynamicProvider: and resolve labelColor inside -performAsCurrentDrawingAppearance: on the appearance it's given. Concentric corners A button tucked into a window's corner looks right with that corner's radius set to the window's minus the gap, 16 − 6 = 10 points for a 6-point gap. Little Dia's buttons get one corner like that with a mask path. They never change size, so the crossfade under Different corners need cornerRadii doesn't come up.

title: Command Bar
text: Part of Discoveries. The new tab page's bar It works on its own The bar on the new tab page is AssistantPanelUIBase.AssistantPanelRootView. Moved into another view, even with its tab in the background, its suggestions, chats, @ and / keep working, and what it opens loads in its own tab. Its "Add tabs or files" button only opens its menu while the new tab page shows, but typing @ opens the same menu. Only a backdrop layer blurs the page Snapshots and CIFilter backgrounds can't see web content, which Chromium's GPU process draws. A private CABackdropLayer with a gaussianBlur CAFilter can. Going back before the first draw Focusing the previous tab from the new tab page's -viewDidMoveToWindow keeps the new tab page from ever showing. But Dia, still switching tabs, then takes the page's WebContentsHostView out of the window. The page keeps showing through Chromium's compositor layer but takes no clicks. The fix is to add the view back before the window draws (a run loop observer on kCFRunLoopBeforeWaiting), pinned to its parent with constraints. Overlays should live in the page's card Dia animates the card's layer when the sidebar slides, so a view placed from outside jumps to the end straight away. A subview of the card moves and clips with it. Closing a window's last tab Dia opens the new tab that replaces it before the old one is gone, so for a moment both are in appleScriptTabs. The Close Tab shortcut in NSApp.currentEvent is the only sign of a close at that moment. Closing a window's only tab closes the window, and Dia quits with it. A command bar opened on that tab should blank the page when it's dismissed, not close the tab. A restored bar is laid out narrow first On a new tab restored at launch, Dia first lays the bar out 28 pt wide, which wraps the input to 87 pt instead of 23. A height measured then is wrong, so measure it again whenever the bar's width changes. Shortcuts before Dia A local NSEvent monitor sees a menu's shortcut before the menu does, and returning nil stops it. The sidebar's New Tab button is TabList.NewTabCellView, which acts on -mouseDown:. Setting what's typed The bar's text is an NSTextView. -insertText:replacementRange: over its whole string changes it as typing would, so the suggestions follow, and -selectAll: then leaves it selected to type over. ⌘L's bar It's the same panel Open Command Bar puts an AssistantPanelRootView in a DynamicPopover root view on the window's frame view, set up to edit the current tab. It can be moved out like the new tab page's, and closes with the popover. cancelOperation: sent to its text view closes it as Escape does. A new one is made each time. It has its own style - Its text is 13 points where the new tab page's is 16, kept in BoostCommandBar.TextContainerView's font ivar. - The first Double of BoostCommandBar.RootView's layoutConfiguration (the space above the text) is 19 where the new tab page's is 21. Dia writes the 19 back a few times while it opens, after sizing the bar by it. - It builds the bar over about 90 ms, from a 30 point strip to full height, then fades the toolbar in over 0.16 s. The toolbar's alphaValue turning 1 marks it built. The popover's root view tells when it opens and closes Its -viewDidMoveToWindow runs with a window as the bar opens and without one as it closes, so the bar can be lifted out and put back there. The popover hides the bar's own ShadowView, drawing its shadow itself, so a lifted bar needs it shown again. Skipping Dia's own animations Removing every animation from the bar's layer tree (-removeAllAnimations, recursively) drops the fades Dia already started, and the bar shows as it ends up. The placeholder The field is an ARCUI.TextViewWithPlaceholder. Dia sets "Ask anything…" from Swift, so hooking -setPlaceholderAttributedString: sees nothing. Hook the getter, -placeholderAttributedString, which AppKit reads to draw it. Hiding a suggestion The list is an NSTableView in BoostCommandBar.SuggestionsView, fed by a diffable data source. Asking it for a row's view while it updates throws and crashes Dia, so look at rows after -endUpdates and -reloadData. The chat row is the one with an NSImageView labelled "chat". -hideRowsAtIndexes:withAnimation: hides it with nothing left behind, but the list keeps its height for every row, so a gap stays at the bottom. Dia keeps its own idea of the selected suggestion, so landing on a hidden row has to move on with moveUp: or moveDown: on the field. Chat's menu items Dia hides and shows some chat menu items itself, so a tweak hiding them should hook -[NSMenuItem setHidden:], keep what Dia asked for, and add its own. Dia runs those items' shortcuts, custom ones included, before the menus, so a hidden item's shortcut still works until a local key monitor takes it.

title: Sidebar
text: Part of Discoveries. The sidebar that floats over the page While tabs are hidden, it's FloatingSidebarContainerView, a separate popover with its own tint and effect views. Restyle it on its own, not through the window. Dia sets its corner radius outside layout A layout hook alone loses the change half the time. Watch the layer's cornerRadius with KVO, and reapply when it changes. The header stack keeps room for hidden views Hiding the traffic lights (ARCUI.WindowStandardButtons) leaves a gap. -setVisibilityPriority:NSStackViewVisibilityPriorityNotVisible forView: closes the gap and can be undone. Changing detachesHiddenViews drops the view from the stack for good. The stack also keeps its 18 pt leading inset once the traffic lights are gone, so the profile button ends up 12 pt in from the pinned tabs. Move the stack in the header's own layout, after Dia has placed it, so no other stack view is touched. Dia hides some header views as the window appears In Dia 1.56 it hides the recent tabs button that way, but only if the button says it's showing. One a tweak already hid gets skipped, and comes back as a second button when the tweak is turned off. Until the window is visible, answer NO from -isHidden to callers in Dia's own code (dladdr on the return address) for views the tweak hid. Answering AppKit too shows the view, and answering after the window shows leaves an empty space where the view was. Profile dots SpaceSwitcherItemView redraws selection in -updateLayer, not -layout. Dia also moves the items outside layout, so spacing changes belong in -setFrame:. Profiles are keyed by spaceID, which survives renames. The footer centers SpaceSwitcherView between its Chats and Recent Tabs buttons, so hiding one of them pulls the dots off center. After the footer lays out, give the switcher the wider of its two gaps on both sides. Pinned tab border The colored border round the selected pinned tab is its own view, SelectionOutlineView, inside each TabDockItemView. The tab list It's a collection view, TabList.TabListView.CollectionView, laid out by TabList.TabListCollectionViewLayout. Section 0 is the pinned tabs and folders, and its last item is a short row that draws the line under them (Dia's Close All line). Section 1 is today's tabs and section 2 is New Tab. The profile is viewModel.delegate.spaceID on the TabList.TabListView. Moving rows in the tab list Wrapping the layout's -prepareLayout, -layoutAttributesForItemAtIndexPath:, -layoutAttributesForElementsInRect: and -collectionViewContentSize moves rows without Dia knowing. A hidden row should be left out of the elements in a rect, or the list keeps a see-through view for it that still catches the pointer. Animate with performBatchUpdates: on the list's animator, invalidating the layout inside it. Drops follow Dia's own layout Dia works out where a dragged tab lands from its own row positions, so with rows moved, wrap the TabList.TabListView dragging methods and hand Dia an NSProxy of the drag with the pointer moved back. Dia pins a tab dropped above the middle of the first tab after the line.

title: Tabs and Windows
text: Part of Discoveries. Tab order appleScriptWindows and then appleScriptTabs list tabs in on-screen order, with tabId, URL and close:. Moving tabs The browser delegate can create tab groups, add and remove tabs, and run moveTabGroupWithId:toNewIndex:. The group index counts from the first unpinned tab. To move a single tab, put it alone in a temporary group, move the group, then ungroup it. Front window The key window is often Settings or a popover. Walk NSApp.orderedWindows front to back for the first browser window. Tab switcher (⌃⇥) RecentTabsWindowController keeps its list in viewModel.stateSubject.currentValue, and doesn't refresh while open. It commits as soon as a ⌘ flag change arrives, before local event monitors run. To catch ⌘W in it, hook -[NSApplication nextEventMatchingMask:untilDate:inMode:dequeue:]. Downloads Dia opens the downloads list itself when a download starts, usually while the click on the page's link is still the current event. To tell that apart from the user asking, check the click is on the button, and count -accessibilityPerformPress too, as VoiceOver and Full Keyboard Access use it. Native messaging hosts They're started with posix_spawn. Interposing it lets a tweak start a different helper. A tab's page A sidebar tab is a TabUI.TabView. Its contentViews hold a TabContentView per page (more than one for a split), and each one's viewModel.delegate is a TabContentController with the tab's contentID and webContentURL. It doesn't lead to the page itself, an ArcWebContents, and none of the page's own IDs match the tab's contentID. Collect pages from -[ArcWebContents setVisibility:], which every page gets, and match them by URL, only when one page has it. Unloading a page -[ArcWebContents discard] asks Chromium to drop the page. The answer comes to the page's delegate, ADK.WebContentChromium, as -webContents:finalizeDiscardRequest: with a BOOL. Chromium says no for a page playing audio or one on screen. -visibility is 0 hidden, 1 occluded or 2 visible. Closing a page A page made with createWebContents: is closed with -close. With some extensions installed (Quillbot is one), closing a page that still shows a site crashes Dia inside ArcCore, on a null pointer. Dia closes its own tabs with -closeWithForegroundCommitTiming:1, but that crashes too, and so do closing later or closing right after starting a load of about:blank. What works is loading about:blank, waiting until the page's url is about:blank (about 50 ms), and only then closing it. Selecting a tab doesn't lay it out The tab's view doesn't get -layout when it's selected, so a tweak can't notice there. Its page's setVisibility: with 2 is the cue. Whether a tab is selected is in its viewModel.stateSubject.currentValue, as selectionStyle. Menu icons on macOS 27 An NSMenuItem's image is hidden unless its preferredImageVisibility is .visible. Dia's own tab menu items set it, so an added item without it shows no icon and sits further left than the rest. The property is new in the macOS 27 SDK, so a build with an older SDK, like the one CI uses, doesn't know it: set it by name, [item setValue:@1 forKey:@"preferredImageVisibility"] inside @available(macOS 27, ), where 1 is .visible. Where a link goes Every link and window.open is asked about in -[ADK.WebContentChromium webContents:decidePolicyForNavigationAction:], which returns a disposition: 0 ignore, 1 this tab, 2 a new tab in front, 3 a new tab behind (⌘-click), 5 a new window (Shift-click) and 6 a popup (window.open with a size). The action's navigationDisposition is what the page asked for. To make a new-tab link stay in its page, pass Dia an NSProxy around the action whose navigationDisposition is 1: no other page is made, and tweaks that look at links, like Peek, see an ordinary link. A popup with a size skips this and opens its own window, which sign-in pages need. A new tab from a popup window A popup window has no tabs, so a new-tab link in it opens a tab in a normal window and brings that window forward. Little Arc opens such links in hidden tabs instead, so ⌘W shows the page before. didCreateNewWebContent -[ADK.WebContentChromium webContents:didCreateNewWebContent:targetURL:disposition:] is shared by every page. Its first argument is the page that opened the new one, an ArcWebContents; self isn't. Coming forward for a link A link clicked in another app makes macOS bring Dia forward before the link arrives. With Dia hidden, it comes in this order, about 100 ms apart overall: will unhide, did unhide, will become active, did become active, and only then the GURL Apple event. Every window shows for that moment. To show only some, make the others see-through in NSApplicationWillUnhideNotification (alphaValue 0), and put them back after the event, or after a quarter of a second if none comes.

title: Password Managers
text: Part of Discoveries. Helpers check who started them Apple's Passwords helper has a launch constraint, and 1Password's helper checks the parent browser's code signature. A patched Dia, signed on your Mac, passes neither, but the original Dia, kept unpatched, passes both. 1Password's helper is sandboxed It can only read apps under /Applications. A clone there (clonefile, instant on APFS) works; one in ~/Library doesn't. Launch Services registers any app in /Applications Hidden folders included, and it may then send links and "open Dia" to it. Run lsregister -u on the copy after starting it.

title: Settings
text: Part of Discoveries. SF Symbols differ between macOS versions A symbol name that's new in macOS 27, such as circle.on.app.liquid.glass.fill, gives nil on macOS 26, and +[NSImageView imageViewWithImage:nil] throws, which took down the whole Settings pane. Give each icon older fallbacks and use the first that exists. /System/Library/CoreServices/CoreGlyphs.bundle/Contents/Resources/name_availability.plist lists the year each symbol arrived, and its year_to_release maps each year to a macOS version (2025 is macOS 26, 2026 is macOS 27), so you can check a name without an older Mac. Glass hints instead of tooltips macOS 26's hints, the glass bubbles with an arrow that System Settings shows, are an NSPopover with a label in it. A few things it needs: - Give the content view its fittingSize as its frame, and the view controller its preferredContentSize, before showing it. Otherwise a wrapping label lays out at zero width and the popover opens as a tall sliver. - NSPopoverBehaviorTransient closes it on any click, and the click still reaches what it was aimed at, such as a Settings row. - An NSTrackingArea doesn't retain its owner. Keep the owner alive with the view, and remove the area before letting the owner go. DPSetHint in StdPatch does all of this. Resizable turns on the green button The Patches pane makes the Settings window resizable so it can grow taller, and that turns on the green button, which then zooms or goes full screen. Disable NSWindowZoomButton and set NSWindowCollectionBehaviorFullScreenNone while the pane shows, and put both back when it goes. Rows that appear slide over the row above Unhiding a row in an NSStackView while an animation is running makes it ride down from the top of its group over the row above, and hiding one inside an animation fades it out while it moves, which leaves a ghost behind. Hide or unhide inside an NSAnimationContext group with a duration of 0 and allowsImplicitAnimation off, so only the rows around it slide. A row that appears starts at alpha 0 and fades in once the gap has opened, about 0.2 seconds later. Take its separator with it, the view before it in arrangedSubviews. Recording a shortcut Settings' shortcut field, like the one on Dia's Shortcuts page, records with a local NSEvent monitor for key-down events while it's recording, and returns nil from it so the keys don't reach Dia. It saves the key code, the modifier flags masked to ⌘⌃⌥⇧, and the characters for showing it. Ask for ⌘, ⌃ or ⌥ unless it's a function key, or plain letters get taken from text fields. Delete clears it and Escape cancels. DPShortcutField and DPShortcutMatches in StdPatch do this. Sections and headings Settings sorts its sections by the order of each section's first tweak, and lists Hide tweaks last in each, shortest title first. An option, a tweak with requires, shows on its parent's page instead, under a heading named by its own section, or Options if it has none. A parent's own rows go under the heading their view's identifier names. Options this Dia can't use go in Not Available in This Version, last. Making Patches open quickly With about 60 rows, building the pane and laying it out took about 370 ms. What cost most: - -[NSSwitch intrinsicContentSize], about a quarter of layout. Every switch here is the same small one, so cache it. - NSBox separators. A one-point view with separatorColor, its alignmentRectInsets set to (0.5, 0, -0.5, 0), draws the same line in the same place. - Building a new symbol image per row. Look each one up and size it once, with -imageWithSymbolConfiguration:, and share it. Laying a view out before it's in the window doesn't carry over: adding it costs about as much again. Adding it hidden as Settings opens and showing it on click takes about 5 ms. Hiding Dia's own rows The sidebar (Preferences.SidebarListView) doesn't implement -tableView:heightOfRow:, and Shortcuts and Advanced are NSTableViews too. -hideRowsAtIndexes:withAnimation: hides rows in all of them. Unhide with the table's own hiddenRowIndexes: indexes saved earlier can point past the end after the list changes, and unhiding those crashes Dia.

title: Apple Intelligence
text: Part of Discoveries. "Model not ready" doesn't always mean downloading SystemLanguageModel.default.availability in FoundationModels has only three reasons it can't run: deviceNotEligible, appleIntelligenceNotEnabled and modelNotReady. It reports modelNotReady both while the model downloads and when macOS will never download it, because a setting rules Apple Intelligence out. In the second case nothing is under /System/Library/AssetsV2/ for the language model, and waiting doesn't help. macOS's eligibility check says which setting Apple Intelligence's internal name is GREYMATTER. macOS decides whether a Mac may have it in libsystem_eligibility, which every process can call: c long domain = os_eligibility_domain_for_name("OS_ELIGIBILITY_DOMAIN_GREYMATTER"); // 122 on macOS 27 uint64_t answer, source; xpc_object_t status, context; // both come back retained os_eligibility_get_domain_answer(domain, &answer, &source, &status, &context); answer is 4 when the Mac is eligible and 2 when it isn't. status maps each input it checked to 3 if it passed and 2 if it failed: Input Fails when --- --- DEVICE_CLASS, GENERATIVE_MODEL_SYSTEM The Mac can't run it EXTERNAL_BOOT_DRIVE The Mac started up from an external drive COUNTRY_LOCATION, COUNTRY_BILLING It isn't offered in the country or region DEVICE_REGION_CODE The Mac's region in Language & Region DEVICE_LANGUAGE The Mac's language isn't supported SIRI_LANGUAGE Siri's language isn't supported DEVICE_AND_SIRI_LANGUAGE_MATCH Siri and the Mac use different languages context holds the languages it compared: OS_ELIGIBILITY_CONTEXT_ELIGIBLE_SIRI_LANGUAGE and OS_ELIGIBILITY_CONTEXT_ELIGIBLE_DEVICE_LANGUAGES. The Mac's side isn't simply its first language. English (US) with the region set to Malta comes out as en-GB, so with Siri on English (US) the match fails and Apple Intelligence never downloads, while FoundationModels keeps saying it isn't ready. A call takes well under a millisecond, so it's fine to make on hover. /private/var/db/os_eligibility/eligibility.plist holds the same answers for many domains, but it left GREYMATTER out on one Mac, so ask the function instead. Both functions are private and could change with any macOS update; Tidy Tabs falls back to a general message if they're missing. Other ways in GMAvailabilityWrapper in the private GenerativeModels framework has +isDeviceEligible, +currentWithUseCaseIdentifiers: and more, but only says whether, not why. Finding the domain number came from setting a breakpoint on os_eligibility_get_domain_answer while calling +isDeviceEligible.

title: Testing
text: Part of Discoveries. Dev notifications With devTools on, com.diapatches.dev.set flips a tweak, and com.diapatches.dev.dump writes every window's view tree to views.txt beside the dylib. Tab layout without clicking It's saved per window in the persistedWindowData default, as "tabLayoutStyle":{"sidebar":{}} or {"tabStrip":{}}. Up to Dia 1.55 you could edit it while Dia was quit; Dia 1.56 ignores the edit. View → Show Tabs in Sidebar switches the front window while Dia runs, and its checkmark (AXMenuItemMarkChar) says which layout that window has. Clicked while a new window's command bar is still open, it does nothing. New windows, and windows restored after a relaunch, take the layout last chosen, so switch a throwaway window back to the sidebar when you're done. Clicked through System Events while Dia is in the background, it does nothing, even after AXRaise on the window: activate Dia first. make test reports tabs in the sidebar if any visible window has them, so switch each one. Driving Dia from a script - Test in a new window of your own, and check it's in front before every keystroke. A window that's open at the start is someone's real tabs. - System Events' ⌘T doesn't open a new tab in a second window. Clicking File → New Tab does. - With several windows open, read state from the key window only. The first window in NSApp.windows is often another one. - Tooltips and hover hints only come up for real mouse-moved events. Warping the pointer moves it without one, so post kCGEventMouseMoved events along a path instead. - A window closed just before Dia quits can come back at the next launch. Check the window list after a relaunch. - A window's position doesn't tell yours from a test window. A new window opens at the same spot as a full-size one. Count windows before and after, and remember the new window's ID. - The Settings window has no title. Pick a pane with System Events' set selected of row N of table 1 of scroll area 1 of splitter group 1. Its scroll bar isn't exposed, so scroll with pixel scroll-wheel events. - A page waiting on an image the server answers after a few seconds keeps loading that long, which is enough to see loading progress. Crashes that need an extension Some crashes only happen with a certain extension installed. Install it in a separate test profile, so nobody's own profile runs it, and remove it from chrome://extensions when done. macOS's crash dialog belongs to the UserNotificationCenter process; its Ignore button dismisses it. Putting settings back defaults import merges into the domain rather than replacing it, so keys a test added stay behind. Note each key's old value before a test and write it back after. Catching a one-frame glitch Screenshots in a loop are too slow. Record the window alone with ScreenCaptureKit at 120 fps, compare frames to the resting one, and always record stock Dia (tweak off) as well. Several glitches turned out to be Dia's own. Installing a build Copy the dylib to a new file, then mv it over the installed one. Copying over it in place makes Dia die with "Code Signature Invalid". The number of scenarios moves make test's pairwise scenarios are picked greedily in Settings order, so moving a tweak to another section changes how many there are. Every pair is still covered. Crashes after launch and safe mode Safe mode turns tweaks off when Dia crashes soon after launch. Layout loop crashes came up to 100 seconds in, so it now counts a crash for 3 minutes after launch, not 15 seconds. Four such crashes in a row turn DiaTweaks off completely. After one launch that stays open or quits normally, the next launch brings Settings back with tweaks paused; that happens once per build. Packaging on a Mac ditto -c -k keeps extended attributes, and macOS gives every file a build makes a com.apple.provenance attribute, so a zip packed on a Mac gets a ._ file beside each one. CI's runner doesn't add them. To pack a release by hand, copy the files somewhere, run xattr -cr on them and zip with ditto -c -k --norsrc. CI builds with an older SDK CI's Xcode is older than the Mac we test on, so an API that's new in macOS 27 builds here and fails there. Check the make job on a PR before merging, and reach new properties by name until CI's SDK catches up. Modifier keys get stuck A synthetic click posted with Shift or ⌘ can leave the key down for every later click, which turns them into Shift- or ⌘-clicks: Peek opens and links go to background tabs. Post key-up events for every modifier after any test that holds one. Timing and drawing inside Dia A dev notification can time Dia's own code where it runs, such as selecting a Settings pane, and render a view offscreen with -cacheDisplayInRect:toBitmapImageRep: to compare before and after pixel by pixel. An NSWindow made in code is released when closed unless releasedWhenClosed is NO, and with ARC that crashes Dia. Window order CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo with on-screen windows lists them front to back with their app and number, no screen recording permission needed. It's how to check which windows came forward.
